citations.quote: This paper will review the technical outcomes of a unique two-semester graduate-level Small Satellite Systems Design Course, offered under a collaboration between North Carolina A&T, Old Dominion University, Georgia Tech and Florida Institute of Technology, with additional faculty support from Hampton University and NASA Langley Research Center.

In addition, the course was developed around utilizing Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) practices and tools throughout the design life-cycle while utilizing a common design language, Systems Modelling Language (SysML). The approach started with a mission idea and proceeded to a feasible concept that included requirements development and management, concept modeling and performance simulation, and prototype building using low-cost additive manufacturing techniques, ending with a "Shark-tank" style presentation.

The faculty initially formed four teams, intentionally pairing students from different universities and disciplinary backgrounds to expose them to some of the inherent challenges of collaborating with team members from a geographical distance. The teams were given a set of customer requirements and one of four different global target regions.

The design process and procedure followed the methods outlined in the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook [NASA/SP 2007-6105], as well as the text Space Mission Engineering: The New SMAD. Teams learned and utilized MBSE tools like Visual Paradigm, Modelio, and Magic Draw to structure and organize their projects using SysML/ UML2 syntax and semantics.

Emphasis was placed on trade studies for decision making and all aspects of mission architecture were addressed including con-ops, orbital design and analysis, performance metrics, data budgets, cost, testing, scheduling, sub-systems integration, and preliminary risk assessment. There were three major presentations given to a panel of faculty members and guest experts, each followed by technical questions and feedback: a Mission Concept Review (MCR), a Preliminary Design Review (PDR), and a Critical Design Review (CDR). The result was four unique mission concepts that were feasible and developed enough to present to a customer, the faculty, for selection.

The second semester began with a major de-scoping of the first semester results with the goal of launching a reasonably priced payload, with the same initial customer requirements, as a balloon satellite to an altitude of 30 kilometers targeting the geographical region of the Chesapeake Bay. The teams were reorganized into two teams and used the concept of ThinSat/XinaBox technology as a starting point for the re-design. Utilizing the MBSE methods learned in semester one, the missions were de-scoped and re-framed.

The customer, or faculty, expectations outlined for the design were: 1) Observe and quantify chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) in the target region. 2) Measure sea surface temperature (SST) in the target region. 3) Improve upon the current state of the art for either spatial resolution, temporal resolution or both. 4) Added functionality or value is desired, but not required. 5) Reduced cost is desired, but not required.

Following MBSE principles, each team began the system design process with a stakeholder analysis, which led to four unique mission concepts based on their interpretation of the customer requirements. Additionally, for each of the three required presentations the teams provided trade study results for each decision as required. Evidence of their MBSE approach includes Block Definition Diagrams and Internal Block Diagrams utilized to illustrate mission design context and subsystems integration.

The constellation concept will provide a temporal resolution of 5 passes/day. Each 6U satellite in the constellation will utilize deployable solar arrays and a battery for power, and carry a scientific payload of:

This mission will utilize two 6U CubeSats. The result will be a lower cost mission that utilizes COTS products to produce the images with the expected improvements. Each satellite will use a battery and fixed solar panels for power.

The SPACE GOAT mission included a constellation of three 6U CubeSats in a circular orbit with an offset of $ 60^{\circ} $ between the Right Ascension of the Ascending Node (RAAN) of each satellite. Together they will observe ocean color and sea surface temperature of the primary region of Trinidad and Tobago as well as other secondary regions of scientific interest along the satellites orbital path. Along with fixed solar panels and a battery for power, each satellite would be have a payload including:

The BioScope Mission consists of a train of 2 satellites in a circular orbit about the earth at an inclination of $ 7 0^{\circ} $ and an altitude of 422km. Together they will observe ocean color, SST, and provide access to a wide range of scientific data and images appealing to the science community as well as the private sector. Each satellite has a 6U CubeSat structure housing state of the art imagers with fixed solar panels and battery.

The final presentation of the first semester was the Critical Design Review (CDR). In this presentation teams were required to demonstrate the continuity of their project design management through the MBSE methods learned, with a focus on subsystems integration. Also required by the course instructors was a preliminary risk analysis. Some methods used were Fault Tree Analysis and the Risk Assessment Matrix.

All four teams followed a Model Based Systems Engineering approach for the organization and design process of their mission concepts. The tools needed for following this approach were incorporated into the seminar-styled lectures throughout the first semester and delivered by guest lecturers having a specialized expertise with these tools. The teams used these methods for overall project management, to conduct trade studies for decision making, to demonstrate subsystems interconnections and integration, and to begin the risk assessment process.

citations.quote: The new scope limited the missions to a high-altitude balloon launch versus the low earth orbits previously planned for by each team; additionally a major reduction in cost was mandated to make the launch feasible and attainable in the semester time frame. The new teams, ICE $ ^{2} $ BayBSAT and BioGOAT, were faced with the challenge of reducing cost while maintaining as much of the primary and secondary objectives from the model missions of the first semester. This prompted new payload instrument selections and a re-design of the subsystems. The new target region for both teams was assigned as the Chesapeake Bay and the design altitude for the balloon is 30 km. At each presentation the teams used their previously established MBSE derived project management framework to incorporate the de-scoping parameters.

At the start of the de-scoping process, funding was still to be determined. This affected the re-design process and resulted in an evolution of the design over the course of the semester. The new BalloonSat concept enabled an immediate reduction in cost as the lower altitude of 30 km allowed for less expensive imagers to achieve comparable spatial resolutions.

Additionally, both teams made multiple iterations of budget reductions and submitted them to course instructors to facilitate the securing of further funding. The final word on funding came on April 25 with additional contributions from the National Institute of Aerospace and Science and Technology Corporation (STC) of Hampton, VA totaling $1500. This process created a time delay for the ordering of equipment and, consequentially, has delayed the launch tentatively until later in May.
ICE $ ^{2} $ BayBSAT's primary focus for the de-scoping was cost reduction, which required a simplification of mission objectives.

BioGOAT's new mission concept focused on balancing the lower cost with the original concept of providing added functionality from the BioScope first semester design. The payload will include a MAPIR VNIR Imager that will provide images with 3 bands of information in the 850nm (NIR), 550nm (Green), and 475nm (Blue) ranges. Also included in the payload will be a First-Person View camera. BioGOAT's BalloonSat will be able to determine altitude by sensing atmospheric pressure as well as direction, with an additional sensor that will serve as a digital compass. The mission will be controlled by a raspberry pi3 and supported with XinaBox sensors. Images will be transmitted at regular intervals during the mission, while images taken between transmission will be processed on recovery. The main housing will be a 3D printed chassis (Figure 14) with Styrofoam panels for insulation.

Utilizing the project management approach of Model Based Systems Engineering provided students with valuable real-world knowledge and experience that will be useful in both the research and corporate environments. The multi-University and multi-disciplinary aspects of this course highlighted the usefulness of the MBSE approach as most engineering projects are multi-disciplinary in nature and modern technology makes communicating with experts around the world nearly effortless.

The main suggestion was to have the funding amount and process defined at the beginning of the build semester. This would allow teams to be more productive during the build semester, and requiring only one design process with a well-defined scope and budget. It would also allow time for purchasing parts with longer lead times and allow them to budget time for more testing.
SCS Gecko Imager providing a spatial resolution of 39m/pixel @ 500km
This mission configuration improves upon the spatial resolution by a factor of 10 and the temporal resolution by a factor of 2.5.

These instruments have spatial resolutions of 72m/pixel for the VNIR, and 183 m/pixel for the LWIR, which represents an improvement of approximately 5 times the current standard. Additionally, the constellation configuration provides a temporal resolution of 8 passes/day, an improvement by a factor of 4.
This configuration provides spatial resolutions of 19m/pixel and 84.5 m/pixel respectively at an altitude of 500 km. This represents an improvement of the current standard by a factor of 19.

This configuration provides a spatial resolution of 38m/pixel for the VNIR instrument, 42m/pixel for the SWIR, and 301m/pixel for the TIR @ 422m. This is an improvement of the current standard by more than a factor of 8.

An example of these concept changes is that both teams originally had the goal of including the secondary objective of sensing Sea Surface Temperature (SST), but ultimately eliminated this capability from their mission concepts.

The new mission concept is to employ two small visual imagers: one RGB camera and a second without an infrared filter. These images will be processed after retrieval to provide the required scientific information on chlorophyll-a in the Chesapeake Bay by calculating the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) for each

pixel. The NDVI ratio emphasizes photosynthesis while filtering out solar glare and values can range from -1 to 1. High photosynthesis activity corresponds to an NDVI value between 0.1 and 0.9. The housekeeping processes will be controlled with a raspberry pi3 B+ and supported by XinaBox x-chip sensors.
8MP Images will be produced with 11 m/pixel Spatial Resolution.
12MP Images will be produced with 5.6 m/pixel Spatial Resolution

communications functionality of the primary mission goals has been assured.
